citation.title: On Counterfactual Metrics for Social Welfare: Incentives, Ranking, and Information Asymmetry

standing_assumptions:
Setting: a principal-agent model of quality metrics. A principal rewards (or ranks) an agent through a reward function $w$ of the data it observes; the agent chooses a treatment rule $\pi$ to maximize its expected reward; welfare and regret are defined from potential outcomes. Expectations are over the i.i.d. draw of the treatment population, the treatment randomization and, where it is random, the estimator $\hat\mu_0$. The pages of the published PDF carry no page numbers; every location below is a one-based PDF page of main.pdf (28 pp.; pp. 13-28 are the Supplementary Materials). Transcribed from the page images.

(S1) PDF p. 3, Section 2, 'Formal model': 'We suppose that a single agent has access to independently and identically distributed samples of characteristics $X_i \in \mathcal X$ for $i \in \{1,...,n\}$ treatment units (referred to generally as the treatment population). The agent assigns a binary treatment according to treatment rule $\pi : \mathcal X \to [0,1]$, and we use $T_i^\pi \in \{0,1\}$ to denote a Bernoulli random variable indicating the realizations of the treatment rule: $\pi(X_i) = P(T_i^\pi = 1|X_i)$. This framework allows for $T^\pi$ to be either stochastic or deterministic.' 'Let $Y_i(t)$ be the potential outcome if the patient had received treatment $t \in \{0,1\}$. Let $Y_i \in \mathbb R$ denote the observed outcome under treatment assignments $Y_i = Y_i(T_i^\pi)$ under the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) (Rubin, 1980), which implies the consistency and non-interference assumptions. Let $\tau(X) = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)|X]$ denote the conditional average treatment effect given covariates $X$, and let $\mu_t(X) = E[Y_i(t)|X]$ denote the conditional mean of the potential outcome under treatment $t$.'

(S2) PDF p. 3, Section 2: 'We suppose that the principal observes $\{X_i, T_i^\pi\}_{i=1}^n$ (also denoted $\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi$) for all units, and $Y_i$ for all units for which $T_i^\pi = 1$ (denoted $\mathbf Y$). The principal must then choose a reward function $w : \mathcal X^n \times \{0,1\}^n \times \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ with which to reward the agent.' 'Turning to our behavioral assumption, we consider an agent that is risk neutral and maximizes their expected reward. That is, the agent chooses the treatment rule $\pi$ from their set of possible treatment rules $\Pi$ that maximizes $E[w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)]$. Let $\pi^w \in \arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi} E[w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)]$ denote this best response. In maximizing this expected reward, we assume that the agent knows $\mu_t(x)$ for all $x \in \mathcal X$ and $t \in \{0,1\}$. Note that there is no explicit model of the agent's cost here to keep the focus on incentives induced by accountability metrics alone, and all budget constraints are contained in the agent's feasible set of treatment rules $\Pi$.' Appendix B.1 (PDF p. 14): 'Let $\pi^w$ denote the agent's best response for the reward function $w$: $\pi^w = \arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi} E[w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)]$.'

(S3) PDF p. 3, Section 2, 'Total welfare and regret': 'for a given treatment rule $\pi$, we define the total effect of treatment on welfare as $V(\pi) = E[Y_i(T_i^\pi) - Y_i(0)]$.' 'we define the regret for a given policy $\pi$ compared to the best feasible policy in $\Pi$ to be $R(\pi) = \max_{\tilde\pi\in\Pi} V(\tilde\pi) - V(\pi)$.'

(S4) Reward functions. PDF p. 4: 'Reward Function 1 (ATO): $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nY_iT_i^\pi}{\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi}&\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi>0,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$' PDF p. 4: 'Reward Function 2 (ATT): $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi}{\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi}&\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi>0,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$' PDF p. 5: 'Reward Function 3 (TT): $w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi$.' PDF p. 6: 'Reward Function 4 (Weighted TT): $w^g_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi g(X_i)$.' PDF p. 15 (Appendix B.2): 'Reward Function 5 (TO): $w_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^nY_iT_i^\pi$. (1)'

(S5) PDF p. 4, Section 3: 'Assumption 1. The principal accesses an estimator $\hat\mu_0(x)$ which is unbiased: $E[\hat\mu_0(x)] = \mu_0(x)\ \forall x \in \mathcal X$.' The paper's example (p. 4): 'suppose the principal has access to an auxiliary data source $\{X'_j, T'_j, Y'_j\}_{j=1}^m$, with outcomes for untreated patients with $T'_j = 0$, collected from clinical trials or observational data.' Appendix D.2 (PDF p. 21) writes $\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(x)$ for the estimate 'from auxiliary data $\{X'_j,T'_j,Y'_j\}_{j=1}^m$ drawn i.i.d. from auxiliary dataset $\mathcal Q$', with $E[\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(x)] = E[Y'_j(0)|X'_j = x] = E[Y_i(0)|X_i = x]$.

(S6) PDF p. 15, proof of Proposition 6: 'Since $T_i^\pi$ only depends on $X_i$ by construction, we have the strong ignorability property that $\{Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\} \perp\!\!\!\perp T_i^\pi | X_i$.' PDF pp. 15-16: 'Lemma 1 (Optimal Treatment Rule). If the agent's treatment rule $\pi$ depends only on $X_i$, then the treatment rule $\pi^*$ that maximizes $V(\pi)$ is $\pi^*(x) = \begin{cases}1&\text{if }\tau(x)>0\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$' Its proof shows $V(\pi) = E[\tau(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]P(T_i^\pi=1) = \int\tau(X_i)\pi(X_i)dP_{X_i}$. PDF p. 14, Appendix B.1: $\int f(Z)dP_Z$ denotes 'integration of the function $f(Z)$ with respect to the probability measure for the random variable $Z$'; 'the bold variable $\mathbf Z$' denotes 'the vector of i.i.d. random variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$'; $\mathbb 1(x\in S)=1$ if $x\in S$ and $0$ otherwise.

(S7) Several agents. PDF p. 5, Section 4: 'Suppose each agent $k \in \{1,...,K\}$ observes its own sample of $n_k$ patients with covariates drawn i.i.d. from distribution $P_{X^k}$ with the same support $\mathcal X$. Each agent has different treatment effects, denoted by $\mu^k_t(x)$ and $\tau^k(x)$. For rankings to be meaningful, we assume that the untreated potential outcome is the same for all $k$: $\mu^k_0(x) = \mu_0(x)$ for all $k$.' 'the principal publishes score functions $\{w_k\}_{k=1}^K$, and each agent $k$ best responds individually with their own treatment policy $\pi_k$. The agents are then ranked from highest to lowest score function values.' Appendix C.1 (PDF p. 18) writes $\mathbf X^{(k)} = \{X_i^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$, $\mu_t^{(k)}(x) = E[Y_i^{(k)}(t)|X_i^{(k)} = x]$, $\tau^{(k)}(x) = E[Y_i^{(k)}(1) - Y_i^{(k)}(0)|X_i^{(k)} = x]$, $\mathbf T^{\pi_k} = \{T_i^{\pi_k}\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$, $Y_i^{(k)} = Y_i^{(k)}(T_i^{\pi_k})$, $\mathbf Y^{(k)} = \{Y_i^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$, and: 'the principal publishes score functions $w_k : \mathcal X^{n_k} \times \{0,1\}^{n_k} \times \mathbb R^{n_k} \to \mathbb R$, and each agent $k$ gets score $w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)}, \mathbf T^{\pi_k}, \mathbf Y^{(k)})$ after choosing their treatment policy $\pi_k$.' 'We assume that each agent seeks to maximize their individual ranking, and make the simplifying assumption that the agents act independently'. $X_0$ denotes a draw from the reference covariate population $P_{X_0}$ (p. 5).

(S8) Information asymmetry. PDF p. 6, Section 5: 'Suppose the agent observes additional covariates $U_i \in \mathcal U$, and selects a treatment rule $\pi : \mathcal X, \mathcal U \to [0,1]$. Suppose the principal still observes only $\{X_i, T_i^\pi, Y_i\}_{i=1}^n$, and chooses a reward function $w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)$ that does not depend on $U_i$. Let $\mu_t(X,U) = E[Y_i(t)|X,U]$ and $\tau(X,U) = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)|X,U]$. The utility and regret are still defined as in Section 2.' 'Assumption 2 (Bounded Heteogeneity). The effect of $U_i$ on the conditional untreated potential outcome is bounded as $E[|\mu_0(X_i) - \mu_0(X_i,U_i)|] \leq \gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}$.' 'Note that $\mu_0(X_i) = E[\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|X_i]$.' Appendix D.1 (PDF p. 20): '$\pi(X,U) = P(T^\pi = 1|X,U)$' and 'The utility is still defined as in Section 2, and with the additional $U$ variable can be rewritten as $V(\pi) = E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\tau(X_i,U_i)]$.' The proof of Lemma 2 (PDF p. 21) uses 'ignorability in $X_i$ and $U_i$'.

(S9) Readings used throughout; they are implicit in the paper and not printed in these words. The units $(X_i, Y_i(0), Y_i(1))$ (with $U_i$ in the setting of (S8)) are i.i.d.; given the covariates the treatment indicators $T_i^\pi$ are independent across units, with $P(T_i^\pi=1|X_i)=\pi(X_i)$ (in (S8): $P(T_i^\pi=1|X_i,U_i)=\pi(X_i,U_i)$), and independent of the potential outcomes given $X_i$ (in (S8): given $(X_i,U_i)$); potential outcomes have finite means; a treatment rule is a fixed measurable function chosen before the data and the estimator are realized, and the agent's objective is the unconditional expected reward; '$\pi$ is unconstrained' and '$\Pi_k$ is unconstrained' mean that the feasible set is the set of all functions into $[0,1]$ (the appendix restatements say '$\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$'); where no such condition is stated, $\Pi$ is an arbitrary feasible set; $\pi^w$ is any element of the arg max in (S2), and a statement about the regret $R(\pi^w)$ is read for the best response the paper exhibits unless the target says otherwise; $g:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^+$ is read as a strictly positive weight (the proof of Theorem 1 uses 'Since $g(X_i)>0$').

What is and is not a target. Thirteen findings are confirmed errors whose correction changes a mathematical statement, a formula or a proof step, and each has a corrected-statement target: P006-E001 (Major), P006-E002 and P006-E009 (Moderate), and P006-E003, E005, E006, E007, E008, E013, E014, E015, N005 and N006 (Minor). Those for which the validator gave an exact counterexample (E001, E002, E003, E005, E006, E007, E008, N005) also have a counterexample target, and the three rated Moderate or above also have the statement as printed. P006-E009 is a reporting finding that is kept because it rests on an exact identity between two functionals of the same fitted effects, checkable from the numbers printed in Table 1, and the validator proved it in Lean. Not targets, because the correction changes no mathematical statement: P006-E010 (Moderate; the accuracy 0.6824 comes from a scoring line in the notebook), P006-E011 (Moderate; the released Stroke code credits any discharge alive where the printed score says within 14 days), P006-E012 and P006-N003 (code and data), P006-E018 (last printed digits), P006-N009 (the value 0.035 for a quantity computed from the Horse Colic data and the fitted model, not from anything printed), and P006-E016, P006-E017 and P006-N001 (citation, spelling and cross-reference misprints). P006-E004, N002, N007 and N010 were not confirmed, P006-N004 is a clarity note and P006-N008 is undetermined. Of the nine headline claims, P006-H1 to P006-H6 are mathematical and are covered as follows: H1 by P006-T29 (Proposition 1), P006-T1, T2, T26 (Proposition 6) and P006-T10, T11 (Theorem 4); H2 by P006-T3 (Proposition 2) and P006-T1, T2, T26 (Proposition 7); H3 by P006-T4, T6, T27 (Propositions 3 and 9; Lemma 1 is quoted in (S6)); H4 by P006-T14 (Definitions 1-2), P006-T30 (Proposition 4), P006-T7 (Theorem 1) and P006-T5, T12, T13 (Theorem 2); H5 by P006-T8 (Theorem 3, Lemma 2, Proposition 10) and P006-T25 (Proposition 5); H6 by P006-T15, T16, T17 (Theorem 5, Lemma 3). P006-H7, H8 and H9 are empirical results computed from two datasets (Tables 1-2, Figures 1-3) and are not targets.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Assumption 1, corrected to unbiasedness at the treated evaluation observations; Proposition 9 (TT Best Response) and Proposition 3 (TT Regret) under it
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 4 (Assumption 1); PDF p. 5 (Reward Function 3, Proposition 3); PDF p. 17 (Proposition 9 and proof); PDF p. 18 (Proposition 3 and proof)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Assumption 1 as printed: PDF p. 4, quoted in (S5). $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$: Reward Function 3, PDF p. 5, quoted in (S4). $V(\pi)=E[Y_i(T_i^\pi)-Y_i(0)]$, $R$, $\pi^w$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S2)-(S3); $V(\pi)=\int\tau(X_i)\pi(X_i)dP_{X_i}$: proof of Lemma 1, PDF pp. 15-16, quoted in (S6). Proposition 9 and Proposition 3 as printed: target P006-T27. The treatment-population size $n$ is a positive integer. In Assumption 1' and (iv), integrability is with respect to the joint evaluation law, including the random estimator; it is required for the treated residual $T_i^\pi(\hat\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i))$. Pointwise unbiasedness means that each fixed-query $\hat\mu_0(x)$ is integrable and has mean $\mu_0(x)$; this does not itself imply integrability after random evaluation at $X_i$. A jointly measurable random estimator may be represented as $\hat\mu_0(x)=F(Z,x)$ with measurable $F$ and an auxiliary random element $Z$ independent of $(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi)$. Equalities of conditional expectations are almost-sure equalities; no estimator integrability at irrelevant untreated evaluations is added.
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair ('For every admissible fixed policy pi and every unit, require E[hat_mu_0^pi(X_i)|X_i,U_i,T_i^pi=1]=mu_0(X_i) wherever treatment has positive probability, omitting U in the full-information sections. Equivalently, require E[T_i^pi(hat_mu_0^pi(X_i)-mu_0(X_i))|X_i,U_i]=0 ... Pointwise unbiased independent auxiliary estimation is a sufficient implementation') and the validator's derivation, section 5. The moment form is used so that no conditional mean is needed where the treatment probability is zero. The version with $U_i$ is in target P006-T8; the vector version needed for the average reward $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}$ is the hypothesis of targets P006-T2 and P006-T3.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 1 (Incentive Alignment), under the corrected Assumption 1 and with a strictly positive weight
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 6 (Section 4); PDF p. 19 (Appendix C.2, restatement and proof)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w^g_{\mathrm{TT}}$: Reward Function 4, PDF p. 6, quoted in (S4). Lemma 1 and $V(\pi)=\int\tau(X_i)\pi(X_i)dP_{X_i}$: PDF pp. 15-16, quoted in (S6). Assumption 1 as printed: PDF p. 4, (S5); Assumption 1': target P006-T6. $V$, $R$, $\pi^w$: PDF p. 3, (S2)-(S3).
canonical_claim.note: Validator's derivation, section 5 ('With a deterministic covariate weight g, the same conditioning computation gives E[w_TT^g]=nE[g(X_i)pi(X_i)tau(X_i)]. For strictly positive g and the unconstrained policy class in Theorem 1 ... This proves zero regret under (C)'). Under Assumption 1 alone the theorem is refuted by witness A of target P006-T4 with $g\equiv1$. Strict positivity of $g$ on the agent's population is the reading (S9) of '$g:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^+$' and is what (iii) needs. The printed proof writes the arguments of $w^g_{TT}$ in the order $(\mathbf Y,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf X)$ (finding P006-E013, target P006-T14).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3 (Regret With Information Asymmetry), under the corrected Assumption 1; with Lemma 2 and Proposition 10, on which its proof rests
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 7 (Section 5); PDF pp. 21-22 (Appendix D.2: Lemma 2, Proposition 10, Theorem 3 and proof)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
Information asymmetry, $\mu_t(X,U)$, $\tau(X,U)$, Assumption 2, $\mu_0(X_i)=E[\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|X_i]$, $V(\pi)=E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\tau(X_i,U_i)]$: PDF p. 6 and Appendix D.1, PDF p. 20, quoted in (S8). $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$: Reward Function 3, PDF p. 5, (S4), namely $w_{\mathrm{TT}}=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi$. Printed results the proof rests on (Lemma 2 keeps $\hat\mu_0$ inside the expectation, and its second term uses that the treatment randomization is independent of the estimator given $(X_i,U_i)$; Lemma 2 holds only as qualified below, and Proposition 10 holds in its independent auxiliary-data setting, as stated below): PDF p. 21: 'Lemma 2. Under information asymmetry, $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=n(E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\mu_1(X_i,U_i)]-E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\hat\mu_0(X_i)])$.' PDF p. 21: 'Proposition 10. Suppose the principal applies the reward function $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ with an estimate $\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(X)$. Then the regret is bounded by the average bias in the conditional untreated potential outcome estimate. $R(\pi^w)\leq2E[|\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|]$. (3)' The printed proof sets $\hat V(\pi)=\frac1nE[w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$ and bounds $V(\pi^*)-V(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}})\leq|V(\pi^*)-\hat V(\pi^*)|+|\hat V(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}})-V(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}})|\leq2\max_{\pi\in\Pi}|\hat V(\pi)-V(\pi)|$. Auxiliary-data estimate $\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}$: Appendix D.2, PDF p. 21, quoted in (S5).

Lemma 2, qualified. As in (S8)–(S9), $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge1$, $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and $\Pi$ is any feasible set of Borel policies $\pi:\mathcal X\times\mathcal U\to[0,1]$. Write $C_i=(X_i,U_i)$, $H_i^\pi=\hat\mu_0(X_i)$, and $E_\pi$ for expectation under the joint law of the sample, treatment and estimator induced by the fixed policy $\pi$; the law of $(C_i,Y_i(0),Y_i(1))$ is the same for every unit and every policy, and the estimator may depend on the agent's sample. Conditional identities hold almost surely under that law. Consistency, integrable potential outcomes, $P(T_i^\pi=1\mid C_i)=\pi(C_i)$ and ignorability of $T_i^\pi$ given $C_i$ are as in the setting. Assume, for every $\pi\in\Pi$ and every unit $i$, that $T_i^\pi H_i^\pi$ and $\pi(C_i)H_i^\pi$ are absolutely integrable and that $E_\pi[(T_i^\pi-\pi(C_i))H_i^\pi\mid C_i]=0$. Conditional independence of $T_i^\pi$ and $H_i^\pi$ given $C_i$ implies this moment identity on that integrability domain; when $H_i^\pi$ itself is integrable, the identity is equivalent to the factorization $E_\pi[T_i^\pi H_i^\pi\mid C_i]=\pi(C_i)E_\pi[H_i^\pi\mid C_i]$. Then, in place of the printed $n$-times formula,
\[
E_\pi[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(E_\pi[\pi(C_i)\mu_1(C_i)]-E_\pi[\pi(C_i)H_i^\pi]\bigr)\qquad(\pi\in\Pi).
\]
Under these hypotheses, for each fixed $\pi\in\Pi$, the printed $n$-times formula holds for every fixed unit $i$ if and only if $E_\pi[\pi(C_i)H_i^\pi]$ is the same for all units; a common joint law of $(C_i,H_i^\pi)$ across units at each fixed $\pi$ is sufficient. Conditional independence of treatment and estimator alone does not imply this equality: an estimator computed from the agent's sample can have different means at different units' covariates.

Proposition 10, qualified. Proposition 10 holds in its independent auxiliary-data setting: $\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(x)=f(Z,x)$ for a jointly measurable $f$ and auxiliary data $Z$ whose law does not depend on $\pi$ and which are independent of $(\mathbf X,\mathbf U,\mathbf T^\pi)$ under every $\pi\in\Pi$, with $\varepsilon=E[|f(Z,X_i)-\mu_0(C_i)|]<\infty$; no unbiasedness is required. More generally, it holds under the hypotheses of the qualified Lemma 2 if one probability law $D$ is the law of $(C_i,H_i^\pi)$ for every $\pi\in\Pi$ and every unit $i$, with $\varepsilon=\int|h-\mu_0(c)|\,dD(c,h)<\infty$. In either case $|\hat V(\pi)-V(\pi)|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\pi\in\Pi$, where $\hat V(\pi)=E_\pi[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]/n$, and $R(\pi^w)=V(\pi^*)-V(\pi^w)\le|V(\pi^*)-\hat V(\pi^*)|+|\hat V(\pi^w)-V(\pi^w)|\le2\varepsilon$ for every reward maximizer $\pi^w$ and welfare maximizer $\pi^*$ in $\Pi$.

These qualifications add no hypotheses to corrected main clauses (i)–(iii). Those clauses keep the treated conditional-unbiasedness assumption, with $T_i^\pi(H_i^\pi-\mu_0(X_i))$ absolutely integrable for each $\pi\in\Pi$ and unit $i$. It gives $E_\pi[T_i^\pi H_i^\pi]=E[\pi(C_i)\mu_0(X_i)]$ for every unit, so the factor $n$ is valid there without a common joint evaluation law, without estimator integrability on untreated observations, and without estimator moments under policies outside $\Pi$. Maximizers are needed only for the regret conclusions, not for the per-policy identities.
canonical_claim.note: Validator's derivation, section 5 (the information-asymmetry computation ending in $R(\pi^w)\leq2\gamma_{marg}$). Under Assumption 1 alone the main-text statement is refuted by witness A of target P006-T4 with a constant $U$ ($\gamma_{marg}=0$, regret $\frac12$); in the independent-auxiliary setting of Appendix D.2 the theorem holds as printed. One reader reports that the same argument gives $R\leq\gamma_{marg}$; that sharpening is not printed and is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the two sentences 'On the horses that would benefit, the average benefit was 0.147' and 'On the patients that would benefit, the average benefit of treatment was 0.025', corrected: the two numbers are averages over the whole analysis sample
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 7 (Section 6, 'Horse Colic dataset'); PDF pp. 7-8 (Section 6, 'International Stroke Trial dataset'); Table 1, PDF p. 9, row $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed. PDF p. 7: 'The fitted $\mu_0(x)$ and $\mu_1(x)$ show 62 horses benefiting from surgery and 146 being better off without surgery. On the horses that would benefit, the average benefit was 0.147, which is fairly significant.' PDF pp. 7-8: 'The fitted $\mu_0(x)$ and $\mu_1(x)$ showed 1360 patients benefiting from heparin and 5904 being better off without heparin. On the patients that would benefit, the average benefit of treatment was 0.025.' PDF p. 7: 'This leaves $n=7264$ patients'. Table 1 (PDF p. 9), row $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$: Horse Colic dataset, Utility 0.14695, Regret 0.000, Treat rate 0.2431; Stroke Trial dataset, Utility 0.02518, Regret 0.000, Treat rate 0.1872.

Corrected statement. Let $\hat\tau_i=\mu_1(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i)$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, be the fitted effects on the analysis sample, $B=\{i:\hat\tau_i>0\}$, $k=|B|\geq1$, $S=\sum_{i\in B}\hat\tau_i$, $V^*=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\tau_i\mathbb 1(\hat\tau_i>0)=S/n$ (the utility of $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ in Table 1, whose best response treats exactly the units of $B$, so that its treatment rate is $k/n$), and $b=S/k$ (the average fitted benefit among the units that would benefit).
(a) $b=V^*\cdot\frac nk$, and $V^*<b$ whenever $k<n$.
(b) Horse Colic: with $n=255$, $k=62$ and $\frac{293907}{2000000}\leq V^*\leq\frac{293909}{2000000}$ (the notebook's stored value 0.146954 to six decimals), $\frac{14989257}{24800000}\leq b\leq\frac{14989359}{24800000}$ (about $0.6044$); in particular $b>\frac{59}{400}=0.1475$, so $b$ is not $0.147$ to three decimals.
(c) Stroke Trial: with $n=7264$, $k=1360$ and $\frac{50371}{2000000}\leq V^*\leq\frac{50373}{2000000}$ (the stored value 0.025186), $\frac{672601}{5000000}\leq b\leq\frac{11434671}{85000000}$ (about $0.1345$); in particular $b>\frac{51}{2000}=0.0255$, so $b$ is not $0.025$ to three decimals.
(d) From the printed entries of Table 1 alone: any $V^*\geq0.14694$ and $k/n\leq0.2432$ give $b>0.604$, and any $V^*\geq0.02517$ and $k/n\leq0.1873$ give $b>0.134$.
(e) Corrected sentences: 'Under the fitted model, treating only horses with positive fitted effects gives an average welfare gain of 0.147 over all 255 horses in the analysis sample, with zero contributions from horses not treated', and likewise 0.025 over all 7264 patients; or keep 'On the horses [patients] that would benefit' and replace the numbers by 0.604 and 0.135.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mu_t$, $\tau$, $V(\pi)=E[Y_i(T_i^\pi)-Y_i(0)]$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S1), (S3). In Section 6 the fitted $\mu_0(x)$, $\mu_1(x)$ are taken 'as synthetic potential outcomes' (PDF p. 7), and the caption of Table 1 (PDF p. 9) reads 'For each reward function $w$, we report utility $V(\pi^w)$, regret $R(\pi^w)$, and the realized treatment rate $P(T^{\pi^w}=1)$.' $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}}(x)=\mathbb 1(\tau(x)>0)$: PDF p. 5. The Horse Colic analysis sample: the paper prints '$n=300$ horse colic cases' (PDF p. 7) and removes the euthanized horses (Appendix E.2.1, PDF p. 25); 255 is the validator's count from the released data, and $62/255=0.2431$ agrees with the printed treatment rate.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 4 (Appendix A.2, necessity of estimating the untreated potential outcome), as printed, and the step 'Choose $\beta>\alpha$. Then the set of welfare maximizing policies contains a $\pi^*$ with $\pi^*(\bar x)=0$' of its proof
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 14 (Appendix A.2: Assumption 3, Theorem 4 and proof)
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted. PDF p. 14: 'Theorem 4. Suppose $w$ satisfies Assumption 3. Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of all pairs of distributions $\mathcal D,\mathcal D'$ such that the distributions of $X_i,Y_i(1)$ remain unchanged between $\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal D'$. If for all pairs of distributions $\mathcal D,\mathcal D'\in\mathcal S$, $E_{\mathcal D}[w(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=E_{\mathcal D'}[w(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$ for all $\pi$, then regret is unbounded.' The proof takes '$\pi'\in\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi}E_{\mathcal D'}[w(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$, with $\pi'(\bar x)=\delta>0$ for all $\bar x\in\bar{\mathcal X}$, with $\bar{\mathcal X}$ being a set of measure $\rho>0$', sets '$\mu_1(\bar x)=E[Y_i(1)|X=\bar x]=\alpha$' and '$\mu_0(\bar x)=E_{\mathcal D}[Y_i(0)|X=\bar x]=\beta$' on $\bar{\mathcal X}$, and continues 'Choose $\beta>\alpha$. Then the set of welfare maximizing policies contains a $\pi^*$ with $\pi^*(\bar x)=0$ for all $\bar x\in\bar{\mathcal X}$. The regret is then $R(\pi')=E_{\mathcal D}[(\pi^*(X_i)-\pi'(X_i))(\mu_1(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i))]\geq-\delta(\alpha-\beta)\rho$. Fixing $\delta>0,\rho>0,\alpha<\infty$ and choosing $\beta$ to be arbitrarily high results in arbitrarily high regret.'

Counterexample (validator; exact). $n=1$; $X_1=0$ with probability one; the feasible set is the singleton $\Pi=\{\pi_1\}$ with $\pi_1(0)=1$ (always treat); the reward is $w=w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$, which for $n=1$ is $w=Y_1$ if $T_1=1$ and $w=0$ if $T_1=0$. For $B>0$ let $\mathcal D_B$ be the distribution with $(X_1,Y_1(1),Y_1(0))=(0,1,1+B)$ with probability one.
(a) Assumption 3 holds: under any $\mathcal D$ the arg max over $\Pi$ is $\{\pi_1\}$ and $E_{\mathcal D}[\pi_1(X_1)]=1>0$.
(b) The invariance hypothesis holds: for $n=1$ and every $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, $E_{\mathcal D}[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=E_{\mathcal D}[\pi(X_1)Y_1(1)]$, which depends on $\mathcal D$ only through the joint distribution of $(X_1,Y_1(1))$.
(c) Under $\mathcal D_B$: $V(\pi_1)=1-(1+B)=-B$, $\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)=-B$ and $R(\pi_1)=0$. More generally $R(\pi^w)=0$ under every distribution with finite means, because $\Pi$ is a singleton. So the regret is bounded (identically $0$), contrary to the conclusion.
(d) The step of the printed proof fails with its own constants $\bar{\mathcal X}=\{0\}$, $\rho=1$, $\delta=1$, $\alpha=1$, $\beta=1+B>\alpha$: no policy in $\Pi$ has $\pi^*(0)=0$, and the printed bound $R(\pi')\geq-\delta(\alpha-\beta)\rho=B$ reads $0\geq B$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: PDF p. 14: 'Assumption 3 (Non-degenerate $w$). Assume that $w$ does not always induce a degenerate best response: that is, there exists a distribution $\mathcal D$ such that $\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi}E_{\mathcal D}[w(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$ contains $\pi^w$ with $E_{\mathcal D}[\pi^w(X_i)]>0$ (in other words, there exists a non-measure-zero set $\bar{\mathcal X}$ with $\pi^w(\bar x)>0\ \forall\bar x\in\bar{\mathcal X}$).' PDF p. 14, Appendix A.2: 'Formally, let $\mathcal D$ denote a distribution over $X_i,Y_i(1),Y_i(0)$. Let $\mathcal D'$ denote an alternate distribution such that $E_{\mathcal D'}[Y_i(0)|X_i=x]=\mu'_0(x)$, and the joint distribution $X_i,Y_i(1)$ under $\mathcal D'$ remains unchanged. Let $Y_i$ continue to denote the observed outcome under treatment assignments $Y_i=Y_i(T_i^\pi)$, and note that the distribution of $Y_i$ changes under $\mathcal D'$ as well.' $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$: Reward Function 1, PDF p. 4, quoted in (S4). $V$, $R$ ('compared to the best feasible policy in $\Pi$'), $\Pi$ (the agent's 'feasible set of treatment rules', which contains 'all budget constraints'): PDF p. 3, quoted in (S2)-(S3).
canonical_claim.note: Validator's derivation, section 2; exact check in runs/P006/validate/P006-E003/v1/artifact/check.py. Theorem 4 places no condition on $\Pi$; Section 2 lets $\Pi$ be any feasible set and other results say when it is the set of all functions.
